title: The Tempest
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act I, Scene I — A Tempestuous Sea
openingText: A tempestuous noise of thunder and lightning heard. Enter a Ship-Master and a Boatswain. Master: Boatswain! Boatswain: Here, master: what cheer? Master: Good, speak to the mariners: fall to't, yarely, or we run ourselves aground: bestir, bestir. Exit. Enter Mariners. Boatswain: Heigh, my hearts! cheerly, cheerly, my hearts! yare, yare! Take in the topsail. Tend to the master's whistle.
about:
The Tempest is Shakespeare's last solo play. Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, has lived twelve years in exile on an island with his daughter Miranda. He has become a magician. The play opens with him conjuring a storm to wreck a ship carrying his old enemies — including his usurping brother — onto the island. Over the course of a single afternoon, Prospero takes his revenge, his daughter falls in love, and Prospero finally renounces his magic.

Shakespeare wrote it around 1611 and it was performed at court for King James. It is short — under three hours — and is one of his most beautiful late plays. It has been read as a meditation on art, on colonialism, on forgiveness, and on Shakespeare's own retirement from the theater.

angleCards.title: Prospero's power as colonial power.
angleCards.text: Caliban says "This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, which thou tak'st from me." The play gives him that speech and then doesn't resolve it. I want to read how honestly Shakespeare presents the claim — and whether Prospero's magic is shown as liberation or domination.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Tempest as a colonial text — Prospero arrived on an inhabited island, enslaved Caliban, and called it civilisation. I want to see how much the play knows about what it is doing.

angleCards.title: Prospero as Shakespeare.
angleCards.text: It was probably his last solo play. Prospero's epilogue — asking the audience to release him — reads like a playwright's valediction. I want to follow that thread and ask what it means for the play's themes: the renunciation of power, the letting-go of control.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Tempest as Shakespeare's farewell — Prospero breaking his staff and drowning his book as Shakespeare stepping back from the theatre — and see whether the play supports that reading.

angleCards.title: Caliban's claim.
angleCards.text: He cursed Prospero with the language Prospero taught him. He was enslaved by someone who called it education. I want to track every scene Caliban appears in and assess whether Shakespeare intends us to sympathise with him or merely to observe him.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Caliban — his claim, his language, his degradation — and ask whether The Tempest takes his grievance seriously or resolves it too easily.

angleCards.title: Forgiveness vs. justice.
angleCards.text: Prospero's enemies wronged him genuinely and severely. He chooses not to punish them. I want to read that choice carefully — is it moral wisdom, strategic calculation, or something closer to exhaustion? — and see how the play frames the difference between forgiveness and the surrender of justice.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Tempest as a study of forgiveness — Prospero has the power to destroy his enemies and chooses mercy — and ask whether the play earns its resolution or imposes it.

cast.name: Prospero
cast.description: The exiled Duke of Milan, now master of a remote island through magic. He orchestrates every event in the play — the storm, the arrivals, the romance, the punishments. His final act is to give it all up. Whether that makes him wise or merely tired is the play's open question.

cast.name: Miranda
cast.description: Prospero's daughter, who has known only the island and her father. When she sees other human beings for the first time, she calls them "brave new world." Her wonder is genuine — and her limited frame of reference is the play's most uncomfortable irony.

cast.name: Caliban
cast.description: Son of the witch Sycorax, the island's original inhabitant. Prospero taught him language and enslaved him. His resentment is articulate and earned. He is the play's most morally uncomfortable figure — and arguably its most honest one.

cast.name: Ariel
cast.description: An airy spirit who serves Prospero in exchange for promised freedom. He executes every magical task — storms, music, illusions — and reminds Prospero of their deal. His loyalty is real but bounded; the promise of liberty is the one thing Prospero cannot take away.

cast.name: Ferdinand
cast.description: Son of the King of Naples, shipwrecked and brought to Miranda by Prospero's design. He falls genuinely in love, endures Prospero's imposed trials without complaint, and is essentially good. He is there to make Miranda happy and to knit the political reconciliation together.

cast.name: Gonzalo
cast.description: The elderly counsellor who once helped Prospero survive his exile. His famous speech imagining a perfect commonwealth — no sovereignty, no toil, no crime — is presented as naive by those around him. Whether the play agrees with them or not is left open.

acclaim.quote: The Tempest is a specimen of the purely romantic drama, in which the interest is not historical, or dependent upon fidelity of portraiture, or the natural connection of events, — but is a birth of the imagination.

whyItMatters.title: A Late Style
whyItMatters.body: The Tempest is the work of a writer at the end of a long career. The pacing is patient. The forgiveness is hard-won. The verse is more concentrated than in the comedies and less harrowing than in the tragedies. It is one of the great examples of late style in any art form.

whyItMatters.title: Caliban's Question
whyItMatters.body: Caliban — the native inhabitant of the island, enslaved by Prospero — has been read as one of the founding figures of post-colonial literature. His protest, "this island's mine," is a question the play does not fully answer. Twentieth and twenty-first century readings have made him central in ways Shakespeare may not have intended.

whyItMatters.title: Prospero Renounces His Magic
whyItMatters.body: The play ends with Prospero breaking his staff, drowning his book, and forgiving his enemies. It has been read as Shakespeare's own farewell to the theater. Whether or not the autobiographical reading is right, the moment is one of the great gestures of renunciation in Western drama.
